The ID pass finds no match, but the geometry pass does (same kind, net, layer and coordinates), so kigit shows it as unchanged. A plain text diff would call this a change.

docs.title: Types of changes
docs.text:
Schematic changes are split into three types:

Type What counts Examples Electrical Anything that changes the circuit A part added or removed; its value, footprint or symbol changed; a pin moved to another net Fields only Text on a part that doesn't change the circuit BOM fields like MPN, or the reference Cosmetic Layout changes with the same connections Parts moved, wires redrawn, labels moved

docs.title: One HTML file
docs.text: The result is one self-contained HTML page with the PCB and schematic as tabs. It requires no server which you can open it, keep it, or attach it to a pull request.

docs.title: Further guidance
docs.text:
Follow the given order to see how kigit works from end-to-end:

  • Installing kigit
  • Using kigit Command Line (cli)
  • Using kigit GUI
  • General kigit User Interface (UI) Overview
  • Using PCB viewer
  • Using schematic viewer

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Custom-shaped pads are drawn as their anchor rectangle.
  • Footprint graphics (courtyards, fab) aren't drawn; silkscreen is optional.
  • Zones (copper pours) are drawn from the newer revision only and aren't diffed, because refilling a pour changes its shape every time.
  • Old KiCad 5 boards are parsed but less tested.
  • macOS isn't supported for now.

docs.title: Compare Two Commits
docs.text:
Review what the last commit changed on the board:

cd ~/boards/owl_v1
kigit HEAD~1..HEAD

kigit prints a summary and opens the page:

schematic: parts +1 -0, 8 changed electrically, 1 fields only, 0 only moved; 3 nets changed, 0 renamed, 1 only redrawn

Then:

  1. On the PCB tab, hover a green or red trace to see its whole net and how its length changed.
  2. Click to pin the net, and Esc to let go.
  3. Switch to the Schematic tab and hover an amber part to see what changed on it.

docs.title: Before you commit
docs.text:
Without a range, kigit compares HEAD with your working tree, so you can check your own changes before committing:

kigit

docs.title: With the file text
docs.text:
kigit --source HEAD~1..HEAD

adds the source panel: hover anything to see its lines in the old and new file.

docs.title: Moved or Renamed Boards
docs.text:
If the board isn't at the same path in one of the revisions (you moved hardware/owl.kicad_pcb to pcb/owl_v1.kicad_pcb, say), kigit searches that revision for every .kicad_pcb and picks the one sharing the most footprints and nets with the latest version of your board.

kigit 259cd18..HEAD

warning: pcb/owl_v1.kicad_pcb doesn't exist in 259cd18, using hardware/owl.kicad_pcb
         instead (98% match: 62 of 63 footprints and 74 of 74 nets are the same ...)
warning: the board was moved or renamed: hardware/owl.kicad_pcb (259cd18) -> pcb/owl_v1.kicad_pcb (f038da9)

The same warning shows in the viewer, and the comparison carries on.

Warning

If nothing is at least 25% similar, kigit stops and lists the boards it found instead of guessing.

The GUI follows the move too: the commit list includes the commits from before the folder was renamed.

docs.title: Without Git
docs.text:
Compare two copies of a board directly, e.g. two saved versions of the same project. No git repository needed; the older file goes first:

kigit --files owl_v1_old/owl_v1.kicad_pcb owl_v1/owl_v1.kicad_pcb
kigit old.kicad_pcb new.kicad_pcb              # two board files = --files

The schematic next to each board is compared too. The viewer labels the two sides by file name, or by folder name when both files have the same name.

docs.title: In the GUI
docs.text:
Press Compare folders in the header and pick each copy's folder. kigit finds the board in each (and the schematic next to it), and the viewer opens as usual. 3D in the header shows the boards in 3D beside it, as for commits: New, Old or Both (KiCad makes each from the board file in that folder, with the 3D models in the folder).

Opening a project that isn't in git offers the same thing, with that project already filled in.

docs.title: 3D View
docs.text:
See a commit's board in 3D, the way KiCad draws it: copper, pads, silkscreen, solder mask and the parts' 3D models. It isn't a comparison, just how the board looked then. Put several commits side by side, or dock it beside a comparison.

Needs KiCad 8 or newer

KiCad makes the 3D model (kicad-cli pcb export glb); kigit only shows it. kigit finds kicad-cli on your PATH or where the KiCad installer puts it; if it's somewhere else, set KIGIT_KICAD_CLI to its path.

KiCad What you get 9, 10 The full board: copper, pads, solder mask, silkscreen and parts 8 Copper (tracks and zones) and parts, without pads, solder mask or silkscreen (KiCad 8 can't export those); kigit says so 7 or older No 3D view: KiCad 7 can't export a model kigit can show

A board saved by a newer KiCad than the one kigit finds (say, saved in KiCad 9, with KiCad 8 installed) can't be opened by it; kigit says so. If you have several KiCads, kigit uses the newest it finds (or KIGIT_KICAD_CLI).

docs.title: One commit
docs.text:
In the GUI, pick one commit (or the working tree at the top) and press 3D.

  • Drag to rotate, right-drag (or Shift-drag) to pan, scroll to zoom.
  • Top, Bottom and 3D jump to those views, Fit brings the whole board back into view.
  • Parts, Mask and Silk hide or show the parts, the solder mask and the silkscreen.

docs.title: Following traces
docs.text:
Under the solder mask, traces are faint, in KiCad's own 3D viewer too. Turn Mask off (M) and the copper lies bare, so every trace is easy to follow, with its clearance around it:

Top view with the mask and parts off: the copper itself.

docs.title: Making the model
docs.text:
The first time you open a commit in 3D, KiCad makes its model: a few seconds for a small board, about half a minute for a big one. After that, the same commit opens straight away for the rest of the session.

KiCad doesn't report its progress, so the bar is the time against this board's last build.

Those times are kept in 3d-build-times.json in kigit's app folder; the very first build of a board just counts the seconds.

kigit takes the board, its project file and any 3D model files in the repository out of that commit, so footprints that point at models with ${KIPRJMOD} find them. A board saved by an older KiCad points at that version's library (${KICAD8_3DMODEL_DIR}/...wrl); kigit points those at your KiCad's library (and at the .step models from KiCad 10 on, which has no .wrl), so they show too.

Parts whose model file can't be found at all, such as an absolute path on someone else's computer, are left out. The notifications list them, with the file KiCad looked for.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text:
Pick up to four commits and press 3D to see their boards side by side, oldest first. Turn, zoom or pan one and the others follow, so you see each board from the same angle; hiding the mask or the parts on one hides it on all. Link views at the top (or L) turns that off.

Their models are made at the same time.

docs.title: Beside a comparison
docs.text:
While comparing two commits, press 3D in the header to dock the board in 3D next to the diff, so you can look at both. New, Old or Both (side by side, views linked) picks which. It works for Compare folders too, with no git: each folder's board as it is on disk.

The 3D dock. When the commit list and the review panel are open too, it goes below the comparison.
  • Drag the divider to resize it; double-click it to reset.
  • puts it below the comparison instead of beside it, or back. The first time, kigit picks whichever leaves the comparison more room; after that it remembers.
  • opens it in a browser tab of its own (to put on another screen, say). The dock shrinks to a bar under the comparison, where New, Old and Both still choose what that tab shows. Close the tab, or press Bring back, and it's docked again where it was. If nothing opens, allow pop-ups for the kigit page.
In another tab: only the dock's bar stays, at the bottom.

docs.title: 3D diff (beta)
docs.text:
3D diff beta in the header (next to 3D, while a comparison shows) opens what changed between the two boards in 3D, in a tab of its own. It's new and not fully tested: the 3D view above is unchanged, and is still the quick, reliable one.

The 3D diff, from the top: added parts and tracks in green, changed in amber, a moved part in blue (its old place as a faint ghost), removed copper and a removed test point in red.
  • Parts: added in green, changed in amber, moved in blue with a ghost where it was, removed as a red ghost (taken from the older board's model). A part without a 3D model, like a test point, gets an outline around its pads instead.
  • Hover a part to see what it is: its reference, value and footprint, whether it was added, changed, moved or removed, and what changed (a field's old and new value, moved, pads, graphics). The part gets a white box around it. Ghosts tell you they're an old place. Parts on the far side of the board don't answer through it.
  • Copper: added, removed and changed tracks, arcs and vias as coloured strips on the copper (top or bottom; inner layers drawn fainter on top).
  • The legend in the corner counts them. Changes (C) hides or shows the marks, Fade others (U) fades the parts that didn't change, and Mask, Silk and Parts (M, K, P) work as in the 3D view.
  • It uses the same models as the 3D view, so a board already made there isn't made again. The tab waits while KiCad makes them.
  • The bottom corner says which graphics chip draws the page: a dedicated GPU (fine), built-in graphics (the GPU inside the processor, sharing its memory and power: fine for most boards, big ones may lag), or none, where your CPU draws everything in software and it will be slow. It's the chip your browser uses: laptops with a dedicated GPU often run the browser on the built-in one to save battery. To change that on Windows, go to Settings → System → Display → Graphics, add your browser and pick High performance (or use the NVIDIA Control Panel). On Linux, start the browser with prime-run or DRI_PRIME=1. chrome://gpu shows which chip is in use. With weak graphics, kigit draws at a lower resolution to keep it moving.
  • S shows the same render stats as the 3D view, plus what the diff added (changed parts kept apart, ghosts, strips) and how long it took to load (data, models, building the scene).
  • Zones, silkscreen and the schematic aren't marked in 3D: the 2D comparison shows those.

It works for Compare folders too. If no tab opens, allow pop-ups for the kigit page.

docs.title: If it feels slow
docs.text:
Press S in the 3D view for render stats: how long after your input a frame is drawn, how long each redraw takes (CPU, and GPU where the browser can time it), the gaps between frames while you drag, dropped frames, draw calls and triangles, each as p50 / p95. Copy puts them on the clipboard as JSON, handy for a bug report.

Render stats. (This one ran without a GPU, so its times are high.)

KiCad exports a board as tens of thousands of small pieces; kigit merges them into a few dozen when it loads ("merged on load"), so even big boards turn smoothly. Hiding the parts makes it lighter still.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
kigit --3d HEAD~1 -o board.glb   # the board at HEAD~1 as a 3D model (binary glTF)
kigit --3d -o board.glb          # the working tree

The .glb opens in most 3D tools (Blender, online glTF viewers).

docs.title: Bill of Materials
docs.text:
kigit makes your board's bill of materials when you ask for it: in the GUI with BOM in the header, or with kigit bom on the command line. Nothing runs in the background.

The BOM page with U1 hovered: lit on the board in 2D and in 3D.

docs.title: The board beside the list
docs.text:
On the right, the board twice: PCB (drawn from the board file itself: outline, copper on each layer, pours, tracks, vias and pads) and 3D (the same model as the 3D view).

  • Hover a line: its parts light up on both, with a box around each, and the rest fades.
  • Hover a part on either: its line lights up (the list scrolls to it), with a tooltip saying what it is.
  • Click a line to keep its parts lit while you look around (click again to let go); the PCB zooms to them if they're off screen.
  • Select several, like files in a file manager: Ctrl+click (Cmd on a Mac) adds or removes a line, Shift+click takes every line from the last one you clicked, in the order shown (Ctrl+Shift adds the range to what's selected). Clicking a part on the PCB or the 3D board selects its line (Ctrl or Shift+click for more). All their parts stay lit; a bar under the list counts them, and Esc or Clear selection lets go. With several lines selected, ticking a tracker box on one of them ticks (or unticks) it for all of them, and in Assemble, placing a part on one places every selected line's parts (DNP lines are left out).
  • PCB: scroll to zoom, drag to pan, Top / Bottom show or hide each side, Fit. 3D: drag to turn, as in the 3D view.
  • Resize the panels by dragging the line between the list and the board (or between two of PCB, 3D and Notes); double-click a line to put it back. Sizes are remembered in your browser.
  • List, PCB and 3D in the header show or hide each panel, and Hide on a pane's own bar hides it too. One always stays shown (the list alone, the board alone, any mix). Remembered in your browser.
  • Columns picks which columns the list shows: Qty, Value, each part number field, Mouser and Price (after Look up) and the search links. References always stays. The button is lit while some are hidden; Show all brings them back. Remembered too.

The PCB shows straight away. KiCad makes the 3D model after the page opens (seconds on a small board, a minute or more on a big one; a board already made is reused), with its progress in the pane. Without KiCad, the 3D pane says so and the rest works.

docs.title: What's on a line
docs.text:
Parts with the same value, footprint, part numbers and DNP state share a line, with their quantity and references (in order: R2 before R10). Left out: power symbols, # references and parts marked Exclude from bill of materials. A part in several units (U1A, U1B) counts once.

Part numbers are read from the fields most people use, whatever the spelling: MPN (or Manufacturer Part Number, MFR PN...), Manufacturer, DigiKey, Mouser and LCSC (LCSC Part #...). Do-not-populate parts are those with KiCad's DNP flag, a DNP field, or the value DNP (as older projects did).

docs.title: Finding parts
docs.text:
Each line has Digi-Key, Mouser and LCSC links that open the site's search for:

  • the line's own part number at that site, or its MPN;
  • otherwise, for chip resistors, capacitors, inductors, ferrites and LEDs, the value and package: "10k 0603 resistor" (10kR, 5k1 and 4R7 are written the way distributors search: 10k, 5.1k, 4.7 ohm);
  • otherwise the value, which for an IC is usually its part name.

The links only open the sites in your browser. A part number you've typed in (not written yet) searches for itself.

docs.title: Stock and prices
docs.text: Look up on the BOM page (or kigit bom --lookup) asks Mouser and Digi-Key about each line: stock, price for the quantity you need, lead time and lifecycle (obsolete, end of life...), and for a part that's short or ending, what Digi-Key suggests instead. It asks every site you have a key for. It's the only time kigit contacts a parts site, and only when you press it.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Both are free. The first Look up asks for them, or press Keys on the BOM page.

  • Mouser: in your Mouser account, My Account → APIs, ask for a Search API key.
  • Digi-Key: on developer.digikey.com, sign in, make an organization, then a Production app with Product Information V4 ticked. Its client ID and client secret are what kigit needs. Pick which Digi-Key site the prices come from (digikey.com in USD, digikey.co.uk in GBP, digikey.de in EUR...).

On the command line:

kigit bom --set-key mouser       # paste the key, Enter
kigit bom --set-key digikey      # the client ID, Enter, the secret, Enter, then optionally "UK GBP", Enter
kigit bom --keys                 # which sites have a key (never the keys)

They're kept in parts-keys.json in the app folder, readable only by you. Environment variables win when set: KIGIT_MOUSER_API_KEY, KIGIT_DIGIKEY_CLIENT_ID and KIGIT_DIGIKEY_CLIENT_SECRET (and KIGIT_DIGIKEY_SITE, KIGIT_DIGIKEY_CURRENCY). Keys go to curl (which kigit uses to talk to the sites) on its standard input, never on a command line, and they aren't written to the logs.

docs.title: Looking up
docs.text:
kigit bom --lookup                  # a table per site
kigit bom --lookup --boards 25      # price 25 boards
kigit bom --lookup --site digikey   # one site
kigit bom --lookup --json           # everything, for scripts
kigit bom --lookup --refresh        # ask again, not from the last day's answers

On the page, Look up prices Build qty boards and adds two columns per site: the part (its number, stock, lead time and lifecycle; SHORT in red when the site has too few) and Price (the total, and how many at what each). The header sums up each site. A line without a part number shows N choices: open them and press Use to put that MPN and manufacturer in the line's drafts, then write them like any other edit. Shift+click Look up to ask again instead of using the last day's answers. Change Build qty and the page says to look up again (from the kept answers, so it's quick). Hide the columns you don't want with Columns.

  • A line with a part number (the site's own number, else its MPN) gets that exact part. If the site sells it in several packagings (Digi-Key's cut tape and reels), the one with enough stock comes first, then the cheapest.
  • A line without one (most resistors and capacitors) gets up to five choices from searching "10k 0603 resistor", ranked by stock, lifecycle and package. kigit doesn't pick one for you: put the one you want in the MPN column.
  • SHORT means the site has fewer than you need (the line's quantity × --boards). The price is for what you'd buy: at least the minimum, in its multiples (a reel is a whole reel), at that quantity's price break.
  • Short or ending (obsolete, last time buy, not for new designs): Digi-Key's substitutes show as N instead, marked Direct (a drop-in) or Upgrade and the like, each with its stock and price and a Use button.
  • DNP lines aren't looked up.

Answers are kept for a day (parts-cache.json in the app folder): asking again is instant and free. Mouser allows 30 searches a minute and 1000 a day, so kigit waits 2 seconds between them; Digi-Key allows about 120 a minute and 1000 a day (0.6 seconds). A refused key or a site's daily limit stops that site with a message, instead of trying every line; the other site carries on.

docs.title: Editing part numbers
docs.text:
The BOM is also where part numbers go into your schematic, without hunting for parts in KiCad: hover a line and you see exactly which parts it is, on the board, while you type.

MPN and manufacturer typed in for the 100nF line: marked, and counted in the bar at the bottom until written.
  • The columns are MPN and Manufacturer, Digi-Key, Mouser and LCSC when your project uses them, and any field you add with + Field (Supplier, Tolerance...). Each uses the name your project already uses for it ("LCSC Part #", "Part Number"...), so nothing ends up under two names.
  • Rename a column you added (a field or a tracker): double-click its title, or ✎ beside it in Columns. If parts already have that field in the schematic, kigit renames the field on them too (after asking; the values stay, only the name changes, and Undo puts it back). The project's own part number columns (MPN, Manufacturer, Digi-Key, Mouser, LCSC) keep their names.
  • Type in a cell: it's a draft (marked), saved as you type in kigit-bom.json next to the board (commit it to share drafts). A line's value applies to every part on it. Long part numbers wrap onto more lines so you can read them whole; Enter leaves the cell (a field is one line of text).
  • Column widths: drag a column header's right edge. Double-click the edge to put that column back to its own width; Reset widths (in the header while any is changed, and in Columns) puts them all back. Remembered in your browser. When the columns are wider than the list, it scrolls sideways.
  • Write to schematic puts the drafts into the schematic files; Discard drops them; Undo puts the files back as they were before the last write.

kigit is not a schematic editor, and this can't change your design:

  • It only writes part information fields. KiCad's own fields (Reference, Value, Footprint, Datasheet, Description, and its internal ones) are refused, and it never touches the board file, the wiring or anything else.
  • Each field is the smallest change to the file: an existing value replaced in place, or a new field copied from the part's own hidden Footprint field (so it's hidden too, in your file's KiCad format, KiCad 6 to 10). The rest of the file stays byte for byte, so git diff shows only those lines.
  • Before saving, kigit reads the edited schematic back and checks it's the same design: every net, wire, label and part (reference, value, footprint, position) unchanged, and the fields read back as written. If anything differs, nothing is written.
  • If KiCad has the schematic open, kigit says so first: save there, or write anyway and let KiCad reload it.
  • The files it replaced are kept in .kigit/bom-backup/ next to the schematic (not in git), which is what Undo uses.

Only the working tree can be edited: a commit's BOM is read-only.

docs.title: Builds
docs.text:
A build is a batch of boards you're making from the design: Proto run, 3 boards or December run, 50 boards. Pick one in the Build list next to the title (+ New build… makes one); Design only is the schematic's parts on their own, as the BOM opens the first time.

  • A build keeps its number of boards (the Boards box, where Build qty is without a build; saved as you type) and the revision it's for: the working tree (and the commit it started from) or the commit you opened the BOM at.
  • Each build is a folder next to the board, kigit-builds/<name>/build.json, in git with the project. ⋯ renames it (the folder follows) or deletes it (git still has it if you committed it).
  • The build you picked is remembered for that board in your browser: it's still there when you reload or open the BOM again, until you pick another.
  • What's bought belongs to a build: its trackers and carts are kept in its build.json, so each batch starts fresh. With Design only there are none (+ Tracker and Import cart ask you to pick a build).
  • Buy / Assemble (beside the build) switch between what to buy for it and its boards; the view, and the board you're on, are remembered.

docs.title: Assembling boards
docs.text:
Assemble is for building the boards one by one, each with its own placement sheet: Board → Start board #1 (then #2...: a board is only made when you start it, so a 50-board build doesn't fill up with empty ones; each is kigit-builds/<build>/boards/<n>.json).

  • Placed on #n (right after Value): the line's parts as chips; click one when it's on the board (all / none for the whole line). Its ▾ filters Placed, Not placed yet, Partly placed.
  • Each part you place takes one out of your inventory (when it's in it); unticking it puts back exactly what was taken. A part that isn't in your inventory is still marked placed.
  • Placed on the PCB and 3D panes colours that board's parts: green placed, red still to place.
  • A board is done by itself when every part (not DNP) is placed, with the time; you can also set it. Notes keeps a line about the board (a bodge, who has it). Delete forgets it (its parts aren't put back: they're on the board).
  • In Buy, what's placed no longer counts as needed, and the header counts the boards still to build.

docs.title: Buying for a build
docs.text:
With a build picked (and your inventory chosen), the list shows, per line:

  • In stock: what your inventory has.
  • Ordered: what the build's carts have that hasn't arrived yet.
  • To buy: what's left: needed (per board × boards, less what's placed already) − in stock − ordered; ✓ when nothing is. Its ▾ filters Still to buy / Covered.

The header says how many boards your stock covers ("stock covers 37 of 50 boards", and how many with what's ordered); hover it to see the scarcest line. Your inventory is shared by every build and project, so another build's needs can draw on the same parts.

To order just what's missing: Export CSV ▾ → Which lines: Only what's still to buy (and that many), then the LCSC or Mouser file: each line with its To buy quantity.

When a cart arrives: Import cart ▾ → Carts and unmatched rows… → Mark received. Each row's quantity goes into your inventory CSV (found by its MPN or site number, or as its line's passive by kind, value and package; a row for anything new to you), and the cart stops counting as ordered. A line that matched the cart but had no part number yet gets the cart's (MPN, manufacturer, LCSC or Mouser number) as drafts, so it finds its stock; write them to the schematic, or not. Undo received takes exactly those quantities back out.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text:
Your inventory is a CSV file of yours, wherever you keep it (a synced folder, its own git repo, a USB stick), shared by every project. kigit reads it to show what you have, and changes only its Quantity (and adds rows for parts new to you). It only remembers where the file is, so removing kigit or its app folder loses nothing: choose the file again.

Inventory in the BOM's header: Choose your inventory file… (browse to it) or New inventory file… (an empty one with kigit's columns, where you say). Then it lists your parts; type a new quantity and it's written into the file when you leave the box. Edit anything else in a spreadsheet: kigit reads the file again when you come back to the page.

The format: one row per part, a header row first, columns in any order (names matched loosely):

Column Quantity needed how many you have MPN, LCSC, Mouser, Digi-Key one of these... what the part is Kind, Value, Package ...or these, for passives resistor, 10k, 0603 (resistors, capacitors, inductors and ferrites without a part number) Manufacturer, Description, Location, Notes, anything else yours kept as they are 
MPN,Manufacturer,LCSC,Mouser,Kind,Value,Package,Quantity,Location,Notes
RC0603FR-0710KL,YAGEO,C98220,,resistor,10k,0603,400,Drawer 2,
STM32F103C8T6,STMicroelectronics,,511-STM32F103C8T6,,,,6,Box A,two have bent pins
,,,,capacitor,100n,0603,1200,Drawer 1,mixed brands
  • In stock (a column, once you've chosen the file): each line's stock against what you need (quantity × Build qty), green or red, found by its MPN, else LCSC / Mouser / Digi-Key number (drafts count), else as a passive by kind, value and package (10k, 10K, 10kΩ and 4k7 / 4.7k are the same). ✎ changes the count; + add puts a line's part in your inventory. Its ▾ filters: Enough in stock, Not enough, Not in the inventory.
  • Rows kigit can't use (no quantity, nothing saying what the part is, the same part twice) are listed in the dialog and left alone.
  • Every change re-reads the file first (so edits made elsewhere aren't lost), goes through a temporary file, and keeps the previous version as <name>.csv.bak.
  • Windows: if the file is open in Excel, Excel locks it and kigit can't save; close it there and try again.
  • Received carts add to it (Buying for a build); parts placed on a board take from it (Assembling boards).

docs.title: Notes about parts
docs.text:
Why did you pick that regulator, that crystal, that 0603 over a 0402? + Notes under a line's references keeps the reason with the part.

  • + Notes opens the Notes panel where the PCB was (the PCB button brings it back) with that line picked. New note makes a note about it in reviews/BOM/, named after the part ("1k (R1, R3, R5)"), started with the parts, value, MPN, manufacturer, footprint and the commit you're on, and a Why this part heading to write under.
  • A line with notes shows 📝 N instead: press it and its newest note opens. Clicking a line (to light it up) picks it in the Notes panel too.
  • It's the Notebook: the same editor, saved as you type, the same files. A BOM note is pinned to every part on its line, so it's also one of the notes about R1 when you pin R1 in the viewer, it's on the Reviews page, and search finds it.
  • Pin this line pins the picked line's parts to the open note (for a note about several lines); Pin it here pins what's selected in kigit's main tab, as in the Notebook. Click a pin to show it in kigit's tab.
  • Commit adds a line to the note for a commit you pick from the history (its short hash, date and subject): when the part changed, when it was ordered... In the note's Preview, click the hash to see that commit's changes in kigit's tab (see the Notebook).
  • ↗ New tab opens the notes in a tab of their own, laid out wide; the panel closes, and + Notes on the BOM page then goes to that tab. Hide (or the Notes button) hides the panel.

docs.title: What's ordered: importing carts
docs.text: Fill your carts at Mouser and LCSC (the CSVs from Export CSV upload straight into their BOM tools), then bring each cart back into kigit to see what's ordered.

docs.title: Importing a cart
docs.text:
1. Pick the build you're buying for.
  2. Export your cart from the site: Mouser gives an .xls, LCSC a .csv (.xlsx works too).
  3. Click Import cart ▾ → Mouser cart… or LCSC cart… and choose the file.

The cart shows as a chip beside Import cart, like LCSC cart · 7 rows:

  • Click the chip to see its rows.
  • ✕ removes the cart from the build.
  • Importing a site's cart again replaces it (one cart per site per build).

docs.title: How rows are matched to lines
docs.text:
kigit tries, in this order:

  1. The references in the row's Customer #. kigit's own export puts them there, so this is the surest.
  2. The site's part number (Mouser or LCSC).
  3. The MPN.

Part numbers you've typed but not yet written to the schematic count too.

docs.title: Rows that match no line
docs.text:
Usually passives that don't have a part number yet. An amber bar under the header tells you how many there are: they don't count as ordered until each has its line.

  1. Click Match them… in the bar.
  2. Rows marked ★ have a line suggested by kigit. Click Accept, or Accept all suggestions.
  3. For the rest, pick the line from the row's list.

How suggestions work:

  • From the row's description, by kind, value and package: "MLCC … 0.1uF X7R 0603" is your 100nF 0603 line.
  • Values are compared as numbers: 0.1µF = 100nF, 4k7 = 4.7k, 32.768kHz = 32k768.
  • Or by the part's name inside the row's part number.
  • Only when one line fits clearly better than the rest; otherwise there's no suggestion.

With Keep each row's part numbers ticked (the default), the row's MPN, manufacturer and site number become that line's drafts, so it matches by itself next time. Let go undoes a match.

docs.title: The Ordered column
docs.text:
What the carts hold for each line against what you need (quantity × the build's boards):

  • Green: enough. Red: not enough.
  • Each site's share is shown, like Mouser 10 · LCSC 5.
  • Its ▾ filters: Enough, Not enough, Not in a cart, In the Mouser cart, In the LCSC cart.

docs.title: On the board
docs.text:
Ordered in the PCB and 3D panels' bars colours every part, with a count on the button:

  • Green: the carts cover it.
  • Red: they don't.

So you can see at a glance that everything's ordered before you check out. Parts without a 3D model show as a flat tile over their pads.

When a cart is short, each board still needs every position, so the first positions by reference are filled first. For example, 10 capacitors for a line of four (C1 to C4) on 3 boards is 3 per board: C1, C2 and C3 are green, C4 is red.

docs.title: When the parts arrive
docs.text: Mark received (click the cart's chip) adds the cart to your inventory, and it stops counting as ordered. See Buying for a build. Removing a received cart leaves its parts in your inventory.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Every column you can filter has a ▾ in its header; filters add up, so Placed: not done plus Carted: done plus Mouser: short of stock shows exactly those lines.

  • Trackers: Done, Not done, Partly done (DNP lines aren't part of a build, so they're left out).
  • References, Value and the part number columns (and fields you added): Contains... (type), Not empty, Empty: MPN: Empty is what still needs a part number.
  • Each site's column (after Look up): Found, Short of stock, Ending (obsolete, last time buy...), To choose, Not found, Error or skipped.
  • With a build: In stock (Enough, Not enough, Not in the inventory), Ordered (see above), To buy (Still to buy, Covered), and in Assemble Placed (Placed, Not placed yet, Partly placed).

A filtered column's ▾ is lit. Clear filters (in the header while any is on) shows every line again. The search box and Show work on top of them. Filters last until you reload the page.

docs.title: Tracking a build
docs.text:
+ Tracker adds a tick column of your own to follow a build along: Carted, Ordered, Received, Placed, Tested, whatever your steps are.

  • Tick a line when it's done. Its header counts the lines done (3/12, green when all are). DNP lines don't count.
  • Ticks are kept per part (R1, R3...), so they stay right when a line gets a part number or lines regroup. A line where only some parts are ticked shows a half-ticked box (hover it to see which).
  • Filter by them with the ▾ in their header: Done, Not done or Partly done (see Filtering).
  • Like any column, a tracker can be hidden or resized. Columns → × removes one with its ticks.
  • Export CSV includes them (yes, partly or empty).

Trackers belong to the build you've picked: they're kept in its kigit-builds/<build>/build.json (commit it to share progress), never in the schematic: they're about that batch, not the design. That's the difference from + Field, whose values get written into the schematic. With Design only there are none.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
Export CSV ▾ asks which file you want:

  • LCSC BOM tool (upload it at lcsc.com/bom): LCSC's template columns: Quantity, Manufacture Part Number, Manufacturer, Description, LCSC Part Number, Package and Customer Part Number (the references, shortened to fit: "R1 R3 R5 +4"). Every line goes in: LCSC matches by its own number, then the MPN, then the description.
  • Mouser BOM tool (upload it under BOM Tool in your Mouser account): Mouser Part Number, Manufacturer Part Number, Manufacturer Name, Customer Part Number, Description and Quantity 1. Mouser needs a Mouser number or an MPN, so lines with neither are left out, and the page says which.
  • All columns: quantity, manufacturer, MPN, Digi-Key, Mouser and LCSC part numbers, references, value, footprint, fields you added and your trackers. For Digi-Key's BOM Manager (it lets you match up the columns) or a spreadsheet.

Which lines (at the top of the menu, remembered) picks what goes in, whichever file you choose:

  • All lines.
  • Only the lines shown: what the search box, Show and the column filters leave, so any filter works, e.g. MPN: Not empty plus Mouser: Found.
  • Not Carted yet (one for each of your trackers): to order just what isn't in the cart, or hasn't arrived.

Each shows how many lines it has. They use what's on screen, drafts included, and Build qty (how many boards you're building) multiplies the quantities. LCSC's and Mouser's files leave DNP parts out; DNP in export puts them in All columns. Both sites let you check the columns when you upload, if one isn't picked up by itself.

docs.title: Notifications and the log
docs.text:
The BOM page has kigit's bell (🔔) and Log too, at the end of its header, so you see what's happening without going back to kigit's window.

  • Anything that goes wrong (a cart file that can't be read, the inventory locked by a spreadsheet, a write the schematic refused, a Look up that stopped) is a notification, "BOM: ..." with why, as well as the message on the page. The bell shows how many you haven't seen, the same count as kigit's own bell; opening it on either page marks them seen on both.
  • What got done is listed too, without counting as a problem: a cart imported (and rows that matched no line, with the table), a cart received, part numbers written into the schematic, a Look up finished, a board done, a build made.
  • Log opens kigit's session log, live, in a tab of its own. Everything above is in it, with the BOM page's own script errors if it ever has any, for reporting a problem.

docs.title: Which revision
docs.text: The working tree by default (the files on disk, saved or not committed). Tick one commit in the commit list first to get that commit's BOM instead.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
kigit bom                      # the project in this folder, as a table
kigit bom HEAD~3               # at a commit
kigit bom --csv -o bom.csv     # CSV
kigit bom --json               # everything, with the search links
kigit bom path/to/x.kicad_sch  # a schematic, .kicad_pro, .kicad_pcb or folder
kigit bom --write edits.json   # set part information fields (see below)
kigit bom --restore .kigit/bom-backup/20261118-204925-877   # undo a --write

--write takes a list of {"refs": ["R1", "R2"], "field": "MPN", "value": "RC0603FR-0710KL"} (or - to read it from stdin), or {"refs": [...], "field": "Voltage", "rename": "Voltage rating"} to rename a field on the parts that have it, with the same rules and checks as the page, and prints what it wrote and where the backup is. --force writes even when KiCad has the schematic open.

Without git it reads the files on disk; a revision then is an error.

docs.title: Choosing revisions
docs.text:
kigit                      # HEAD vs the working tree
kigit HEAD~3               # HEAD~3 vs the working tree
kigit c46da63..HEAD        # two commits
kigit v1.0 v1.1 board.kicad_pcb

If you give the newer revision first, kigit swaps them so "added" always means "added in the newer revision".

docs.title: Choosing the project
docs.text:
Run it inside a project folder, or point at one from anywhere with --kicad-repo (short: -C):

kigit -C ~/boards/owl HEAD~1                 # finds the board in subfolders
kigit -C path/to/board.kicad_pro HEAD~1      # a .kicad_pro or .kicad_pcb works too

docs.title: Common options
docs.text:
Option What it does -o FILE Write the page here (-o - for stdout) -n Don't open a browser -s, --stats Print every changed net (and cosmetic schematic changes) --json Write the data as JSON instead of the page --silkscreen Compare and draw silkscreen --source Add the source panel --files OLD NEW Compare two files, no git needed --3d [REV] -o FILE.glb The board at REV (default: working tree) as a 3D model, made by KiCad (3D View) --render -o FILE.png A picture of the board on disk, made by KiCad -V Print the log to the console, with debug lines --log-dir DIR, --no-log Where the log goes, or no log

Run kigit --help for the full list.

docs.title: The example project
docs.text:
kigit example [DIR]

Makes the example project (a git repository) in DIR (default: ./kigit-example) and prints its project folder. It won't write over an existing folder.

docs.title: Bill of materials
docs.text:
kigit bom [REV] [PATH] [--json | --csv] [-o FILE]

The bill of materials of the schematic (the working tree, or REV): a line per part, with part numbers and Digi-Key, Mouser and LCSC search links. --write EDITS.json sets part information fields (MPN, manufacturer...) in the schematic on disk, only those, checked to leave the design as it was, with --restore to undo. See Bill of Materials.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
kigit uninstall [--yes] [--purge]

Removes the kigit you ran: its program, the GUI and the example files (on Linux bin/kigit, share/kigit and libexec/kigit under where you unpacked it; the folders around them stay). It lists them, says what each is, and asks first; --yes doesn't ask. --purge also removes the app folder (logs, recent projects, the GUI's Python), listing what's in it first, with a warning if the example project made by the GUI is there. Your projects, and their reviews, notes and discussions, are never touched: they're in each project's reviews/ folder. On Windows it starts the installer's uninstaller. It does nothing for a kigit built from source.

docs.title: The GUI
docs.text:
kigit gui [FOLDER] [--port N] [--native | --browser]

Starts the GUI in FOLDER (default: here). Started outside a KiCad project, it opens on your recent projects. --port N picks the port (default: 8765 or the next free one); It opens in your browser; --native opens a window of its own instead.

docs.title: Scripting
docs.text:
What the GUI uses, if you want to build on it:

kigit --projects [--depth N]    # KiCad projects in the folder and below, as JSON
kigit --log [--max N] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--kicad-only]
                                # commits (+ uncommitted changes), as JSON
kigit --3d [REV] -o board.glb  # the board at REV (default: working tree) in 3D,
                                # made by kicad-cli (KiCad 8+); prints the path
kigit --3d --disk BOARD.kicad_pcb -o board.glb
                                # the same for a board file on disk, no git
kigit --render -o board.png    # a picture of the board on disk (top view), by kicad-cli
kigit --rewritten HASH...       # still on a branch? if not, commits with the same
                                # author and date (where a rebase put it), as JSON
kigit -n -o - A..B              # the viewer page on stdout
kigit -n --json -o - A..B       # the data on stdout

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Every run keeps a log named after when it started, in the log/ folder of kigit's app folder:

Platform Default folder Linux ~/.local/state/kigit/log/ Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\kigit\log\

--log-dir DIR (or the KIGIT_LOG_DIR environment variable) puts them elsewhere; --no-log writes none; -V also prints the log to the console.

docs.title: GUI
docs.text:
kigit gui                  # start in the current folder
kigit gui ~/path/to/board  # or any folder
kigit gui --port 9000      # on a port of your choice

The GUI opens in your web browser, on Windows and Linux alike. kigit gui --native opens it in its own window instead (Edge WebView2 on Windows); if a window can't be opened, it says why and uses the browser. It only listens on 127.0.0.1, so it isn't reachable from the network.

It serves on port 8765, or the next free one when another kigit GUI already has it, so you can run several at once (say, one per project); the address it uses is printed when it starts. --port N picks the port yourself, and stops with a message if it's taken. Panel widths and other display settings are remembered per port.

This page covers opening a project and comparing commits. Reviews and the 3D view have pages of their own.

docs.title: Landing page
docs.text:
When kigit gui starts in a folder without a KiCad project to open (say, your home folder), it opens on a landing page with your recent projects. Click kigit in the header to come back to it any time.

Recent projects, newest first. Resume compares the last two commits you looked at again.

Each card shows:

  • A picture of the board, rendered by KiCad (kicad-cli pcb render, a few seconds, in the background) when you open the project, and again once the board file has changed. KiCad 8 has no 3D render, so with it the picture is a 2D drawing of the board's top instead. Without KiCad the card shows an icon.
  • When you last opened it, and the last two commits you compared there.
  • Open opens the project; Resume opens it and compares those commits again; the cross takes it off the list (the project itself is untouched). A project whose folder has gone is shown greyed out.

The list is kept in sessions.json in kigit's app folder, with the pictures in thumbnails/ next to it; every kigit gui you run shares it.

docs.title: 1. Open a project
docs.text:
Type a folder or press Browse (folders holding KiCad files are marked). kigit looks for a project in that folder and up to two levels below. It tells you if it finds none, if the project has no .kicad_pcb, or if it isn't in a git repository; if it finds several, it asks which one.

The commit list: your working tree on top, then every commit, tagged PCB / SCH when it changed the board or schematic.

docs.title: 2. Pick commits
docs.text:
All commits are listed, newest first, tagged PCB / SCH when they changed the board or schematic. The top entry is your working tree: HEAD plus any uncommitted changes. Hover a message to read all of it, or turn on Wrap messages (above the list) to show long messages on several lines; the date then sits under the commit hash. The setting is remembered.

What you pick decides what you can do:

Picked Button What it does Two commits Compare The diff of the two (below) One commit Review The commit against the one before it, with a review panel One to four commits 3D Their boards in 3D, side by side
  • Filter commits: how many to list, a date range, and "only commits that changed the board or schematic". If the project folder was renamed or moved, its history is followed through the old folders too.
  • Diff commits manually: type any two revisions git understands (hash, HEAD~3, branch, tag, or LOCAL), for when the commit you want isn't in the list.

docs.title: 3. Compare
docs.text:
kigit diffs the two and the viewer opens on the schematic, with the PCB one tab away. See the PCB viewer and schematic viewer for what the colours mean and how to find your way around.

A comparison. Comparing a commit with the one before it opens its review too (right).

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option What it does Include silkscreen Compare and draw F/B silkscreen (bigger pages) Include source Add the source panel (bigger pages) Compare folders Compare two copies of a project without git (Without Git)

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
Every panel resizes by dragging its inner edge: the commit list, the review panel and the 3D dock. Double-click the edge to put it back. The sizes are remembered.

Each panel can also be hidden for more room, and opened in a new browser tab. The buttons are at the top right of the panel:

Panel Hide Open in a new tab Commit list folds it to a Commits rail on the left edge; click the rail to bring it back opens the same project in another kigit tab, with its own commit list and viewer Review panel folds it to a Review rail on the right edge; nothing is lost, and pressing Review again shows it opens this review's page on the Reviews site, as last written The comparison's sidebar « by the board's name folds it to a Sidebar rail; » brings it back ↗, by the board's name or on the rail: the comparison in a tab of its own 3D view (in the main area) — ↗ New tab in its toolbar (one board, or the side-by-side boards) 3D dock folds it to its bar, under the comparison; the board stays loaded in its own tab; closing that tab docks it again Source panel its Source button with the comparison it's part of

Hidden or not is remembered, like the sizes.

docs.title: Notebook
docs.text:
Notebook in the header is for everything that isn't about one commit: design decisions, research, how a part of the board works, a log of what you did. Notes are plain Markdown files in the project's reviews/ folder, in folders as deep as you like, so an Obsidian vault there works as it is (same files, [[links]], pictures), and they go into git with the project.

The Notebook opens on the right without covering the viewer, so you can keep clicking parts while you write:

  • Your folders and notes, browsed like files: click a folder to go into it, or the path above the list to go back. New notes and folders go where you are. A search box looks through all of them.
  • Rename or delete a note or folder from its menu (a note's title box renames it too). Deleting asks first and says what goes: how many notes and other files a folder holds, and whether any of it has changes git doesn't have yet (those can't be brought back).
  • The note, in the same editor as reviews. It's saved as you type.
  • Pins: pin a part, net or footprint in the viewer, then Pin it here. Unlike a review note, a note isn't tied to a commit: a pin remembers where it was pinned, so clicking it later shows it in the comparison on screen, or opens the one it came from. ✕ unpins.
  • Notes about what's pinned: pin something in the viewer and the Notebook lists every note that pins it (on the PCB or the schematic: footprint C2 and part C2 are the same thing) or mentions it by name. The Notebook button shows how many.
  • N anywhere (outside a text box): a new note about what's pinned, pinned already.
  • Commits in notes: a commit hash in backticks (`b3d7ea1`, 7 to 40 characters) is a link in the rendered note, if it's a commit in this repository. Click it to compare that commit with its parent in the viewer (the first commit: with the working tree). From the Notebook's own tab, or the BOM page's notes, kigit's tab shows it. The BOM notes' Commit button writes them for you; on the Reviews page, a commit with a review links to its review.
  • Notes about a BOM line (why you chose a part) are made from the BOM page: they're ordinary notes in reviews/BOM/, pinned to the line's parts.
  • opens the Notebook in a browser tab of its own, laid out wide (your folders on the left, the note on the right). It still works with kigit's tab: what you pin in the viewer there shows up in the Notebook's tab (for Pin it here and the notes about it), and clicking a pin in the Notebook's tab shows it in kigit's. The side panel closes, so a note is only open in one place.
  • Today's log: one line, added to Logs.md in the folder you're in, under today's date (## 16th November 2026), with the time, what's pinned and the commit you're on.

kigit keeps the pins as one comment at the end of the note, which Obsidian and GitHub don't show; everything else in the file is yours, and opening a note doesn't change it. On the Reviews page, each top folder is a tab and the folders inside it are rows of sub-tabs, as deep as they go.

docs.title: Your activity
docs.text:
The button next to the bell shows your year in this project as a heatmap, like GitHub's contribution graph: one square a day, brighter for busier days (hover one for what you did). Below it: your current and longest streak (days in a row), active days, your busiest day, and how many of each you did:

  • comparisons,
  • reviews written,
  • discussions opened,
  • discussion replies (and marking done, accepting, reopening),
  • 3D views.

It's kept in the project, in reviews/activity/<you>/<this computer>.json, so commit it and it goes with the project: on another laptop, your activity there is added to it. Each computer writes only its own file, so two laptops never get a git conflict over it. You / Everyone switches between yours and everyone's in the project.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
The bell in the header keeps this session's warnings and errors, so you can read them after their pop-up is gone. It shows a red ! while any are unread.

Some notifications come with a list, such as the parts KiCad found no 3D model for.

Open in new tab shows them in a tab of their own that updates by itself; Clear empties the list. Notifications last while the GUI runs; everything in them is in the log too.

docs.title: Session log
docs.text:
The log button shows the session's log file and its latest lines, handy for bug reports. Open in new tab shows it in a tab of its own that follows the log as it grows, with a filter box; warnings and errors are coloured.

The log in its own tab, filtered to "compare".

Logs are kept in the log/ folder of kigit's app folder: %LOCALAPPDATA%\kigit\log on Windows, ~/.local/state/kigit/log on Linux.

docs.title: Shortcuts
docs.text: The button in the header, or ? anywhere outside a text box, lists every keyboard and mouse shortcut, by where it works.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Comparing two versions of a board takes three steps:

  1. Point kigit at a project: run it inside a KiCad project folder, give the folder with -C, or open it in the GUI.
  2. Pick two revisions: commits, branches, tags, HEAD~3, or LOCAL for your uncommitted changes.
  3. Read the page: kigit writes one HTML page and opens it in your browser, with the PCB and the schematic as tabs.
flowchart LR
    A[git history] -->|old revision| K(kigit)
    A -->|new revision| K
    K --> P[PCB diff]
    K --> S[Schematic diff]
    P --> H[viewer.html]
    S --> H

docs.title: Minimal setup
docs.text:
cd ~/boards/my-board
kigit                      # HEAD vs the working tree (your uncommitted changes)
kigit HEAD~3               # HEAD~3 vs the working tree
kigit c46da63..HEAD        # two commits

The page is written to .kigit/ next to the board (or wherever -o FILE says) and opened in your browser. The terminal also prints a summary of the most-changed nets and of the schematic changes.

docs.title: Which way to use it
docs.text: You want to... Use Browse the history and click two commits GUI Compare from a script, a hook or CI Command Line Compare two copies of a project without git Without Git Write down why a commit changed the board Reviews See a commit's board in 3D 3D View

docs.title: Colours
docs.text:
The same colours are used everywhere:

Colour Meaning Green Added in the newer revision Red (dashed on the schematic) Removed Blue Moved (same item, new place) Amber Schematic part whose value, footprint or connections changed Grey Unchanged

docs.title: PCB Viewer
docs.text:
The PCB tab draws both revisions of the board on top of each other.

Action What it does Hover a trace, via or pad Highlight its net, show the net's changes Click Pin the net (click again or Esc to clear) Scroll / drag Zoom / pan F Fit the board / Filter nets Double-click a net in the list Zoom to it

docs.title: How items are matched
docs.text:
Tracks, arcs, vias and pads are matched in two passes:

  1. By KiCad's ID (the ID KiCad gives every item and keeps when you move it; a pad uses its footprint's ID plus its pad number). Same ID and same place: unchanged. Same ID and same copper at a new place or angle: moved, shown in blue, with an optional ghost at the old position. Same ID but edited (a dragged track end, a new width or net): removed + added.
  2. By geometry for everything else: same kind, net, layers and coordinates (to 1 nm) means unchanged.

So moving a footprint or the whole layout shows as moved, not as everything removed and re-added, while re-routing still shows the new and old copper.

docs.title: Silkscreen
docs.text: Off by default (--silkscreen, or "Include silkscreen" in the GUI) since it makes pages bigger. Front silkscreen is drawn near-white, back purple and mirrored, each with its own layer toggle. Text uses a browser font, so it's close to KiCad's but not identical.

docs.title: Zones
docs.text: Copper pours are drawn from the newer revision only and aren't diffed, because refilling a pour changes its shape every time.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text: A review is your note on why a commit changed what it changed: the reasons behind a layout move, a part swap or a new net, written while you look at the diff, and kept with the project. Reviews are plain Markdown files, so they read fine on GitHub, in any editor, or in Obsidian.

docs.title: Review a commit
docs.text:
In the GUI, pick one commit and press Review. kigit compares it with the commit before it, and the review panel opens on the right. (Comparing a commit with its parent opens its review too.)

The review panel: a summary, then notes. The footprint pinned in the viewer shows above the notes.
  • Summary: the commit as a whole.
  • Notes: click a net, footprint, part or bus in the viewer to pin it, then press + Note: the note points at it. Click the note's chip later to show it again in the viewer. Without anything pinned, the note is a general one.
  • Titles: press on a note and its title becomes a text box, like its text.

  • More than one thing, or the wrong one: pin something else in the viewer, then use next to the note's chips. Add what's pinned points the note at that too (a note can be about several parts, nets or footprints), Replace with what's pinned points it there instead, and Make it a general note drops them all. The ✕ on a chip takes just that one off.

    A note remembers the two commits it was pinned in, so it can still show a net or part that commit deleted: its chip turns red and says "removed".

  • Each note shows when it was written and, if it was changed afterwards, when it was last edited.

Press Write (or Ctrl+S) to save. Until then the panel says "Unsaved changes"; if you switch to another commit first, your edits are kept as a draft for the session, and closing the page asks before throwing them away. Reviewed commits get a mark in the commit list. Delete everything in a review (summary and notes) and Write, and its file is removed, mark and all.

docs.title: Writing notes
docs.text:
Text is Markdown: lists, code, tables, links. The text boxes (the summary, notes, and discussion messages) work like GitHub's comment box:

  • Write / Preview: Preview shows it as it will look, math included.
  • Toolbar: heading, bold (Ctrl+B), italic (Ctrl+I), quote, code, link, bulleted, numbered and task lists. Select text first to format it; press again to undo it. Ctrl+Z undoes too.
  • Files: paste, drop, or click Paste, drop, or click to add files under the box. Pictures show in the text; any other file (a datasheet PDF, a scope capture, a log) becomes a link named after it. They're saved in reviews/assets/; PDFs and pictures open in the browser, other files download.
  • Pictures open full size when you click them, in kigit and on the Reviews page (click again or Esc to close). Obsidian's ![[picture.png]] (or ![[picture.png|300]] for a width) works too: kigit finds the picture by name anywhere in reviews/.
  • Links: select the words to link and press (or Ctrl+K), then give the address. Web addresses typed as they are (https://...) become links by themselves.
  • Math is LaTeX, as in Obsidian: $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}$ in a line, or $$ ... $$ on lines of its own for a displayed equation. Prices like "$5 and $10" stay text; write \$ for a dollar sign next to something that would look like math.
  • Tags: pick them from the dropdown: the built-in ones (reason, todo, question, risk) and any tag used elsewhere in the project. Type a new one and press Enter to add it; it's saved as one lower-case word ("Needs Review" becomes needs-review), as Obsidian expects.
Tags, coloured as on the Reviews page.

docs.title: Where reviews are kept
docs.text:
One Markdown file per commit, in the reviews/ folder next to the board:

reviews/
  index.md        every review: ID, commit, date, author, subject (rebuilt on each Write)
  3f9a1c0e.md     one review; its ID is its file name
  assets/         added files: pictures, datasheets, ...
  threads/        discussions, one file each (see below)
  decisions/      your own notes, if you like (see below)

Each review gets an ID when first written, which is also its file name. Commit the folder with the project to keep the reviews with the design.

docs.title: Discussions: asking for attention
docs.text: Notes explain a commit. When something in it needs someone to act, like a part that's too close to a hole or a value to double-check, open a discussion instead, as you would comment on a pull request. Anyone with the project can reply, mark it done, and accept it.

docs.title: Ask for attention
docs.text: In a commit's review, pin what it's about in the viewer (or nothing, for the commit as a whole) and press Request. Give it a title and say what needs attention.

docs.title: Talk it through
docs.text:
The Discussions button in the header lists them, with a count while any are active: red while one needs attention. Open one to see it as a chat, and reply: what you changed, or a question.

Each message shows who wrote it, when, and which commit the project was at.

A discussion moves through three states:

State Means Buttons Needs attention Someone asked; nobody has dealt with it yet Mark as done Done, to be accepted It's been dealt with; the reviewer checks it Accept, Reopen Accepted Settled: the discussion is closed Reopen

Anything you type in the reply box goes along with the button you press ("Moved it 1 mm left", then Mark as done).

If you opened a discussion, next to its title renames it (the chat keeps the old title), and next to what it's about changes that, the same way as for notes: add what's pinned in the viewer, point it there instead, or make it about the commit in general; ✕ on a chip takes one off. The chat records the change ("Now about Footprint Y1, Part C5").

To change something you wrote, press on your message, edit it, and Save. Only your own messages have the pencil (they're signed with your git name). The message stays where it was and shows edited. deletes one of your comments, after asking. Status changes (marked done, accepted, reopened) can't be deleted, since that would change the status; edit their text instead.

docs.title: Linking to a discussion or a review
docs.text:
at the top of a discussion copies a link to it, [its title](threads/<id>.md). Paste it into a review's summary or note, or into another discussion: it shows with a 💬, and clicking it opens the discussion. On the Reviews page it goes to the discussion's page, and it's an ordinary link to the file on GitHub or in Obsidian.

Discussions listed in a review (and in the header's Discussions list) have their own button too.

Reviews can be linked the same way: right-click a commit with a review in the commit list and choose Copy review link ([commit message](<id>.md)). Clicking it in a note or a discussion opens that review. The same menu has Copy review file path (the full path of its file) and Copy commit hash.

docs.title: Mentions
docs.text:
A discussion shows where it's linked from, in among its messages at the time it happened: "Author B mentioned this in the discussion USB-C recessed" (or the review of ...). Click it to go there. On the Reviews page, discussions and reviews have a Mentioned in list.

When someone else links to a discussion you opened or wrote in, the shows an @ and a notification says where (it also pops up). Mentions that come with a git pull arrive the same way, within a few seconds. kigit keeps which ones you've seen in its app folder, per project; the first time it sees a project, mentions already there count as seen.

Nothing is written into the linked discussion: mentions are worked out from the links themselves, so editing or deleting the message with the link takes the mention away too.

If a linked discussion or review is gone (deleted, or not pulled yet), kigit warns you: when you click the link, and when you open, write or send something that links to it. The warning also goes to the session log and the notifications. On the Reviews page the link shows greyed out.

docs.title: Jump to the commits
docs.text:
The commit hashes in a discussion are links (dotted underline). Click one to compare the commit the discussion was opened on with that commit, and the viewer shows what the discussion points at, pinned and zoomed to:

Click Compares a message's at hash where it was opened → that message's commit: what had changed by then Opened ... on commit hash (or the first message's) where it was opened → HEAD: where it stands now

So if a part was deleted along the way, you still see it, marked removed, at the place it was, instead of searching the history for where it went.

docs.title: Across commits
docs.text:
A discussion belongs to the project, not just the commit it was opened on. Until it's accepted, it stays on:

  • every review, under Still open from other commits, so the commit with the fix is where you mark it done;
  • the commit list, as a flag on the commit it was opened on (red: needs attention, amber: done, green: accepted);
  • the Discussions list and its count in the header.

docs.title: Sharing them
docs.text:
Each discussion is one Markdown file in reviews/threads/, written the moment you send a message: there's no Write step. Commit and push it like any other change; whoever pulls sees the discussion, and the GUI notices new or changed ones by itself (within a few seconds). Messages are signed with your git name (git config user.name).

Messages are only ever added at the end of the file, so two people replying to different discussions never conflict. If two of you reply to the same one at the same time, git shows a small conflict at its end: keep both messages.

The Reviews page shows the discussions too, needing attention first.

docs.title: The Reviews page
docs.text:
Reviews in the header opens the project's reviews, notes and discussions in a new tab, laid out like a documentation site: one page each, with tabs, a sidebar and a search box.

Home: counts, open discussions, the latest reviews and recently edited notes.
  • Tabs across the top: Home, Reviews, Discussions, then one tab for each folder you keep in reviews/ (for example decisions/ or meetings/), Notes for Markdown files directly in reviews/, and Tags.
  • The sidebar on the left lists the pages in that tab (reviews by month, discussions by status, a folder's notes by subfolder). On this page, on the right, lists a page's notes or headings.
  • Search (or press /) looks through every review, note in a review, note of your own and discussion as you type. Use Up / Down and Enter to open a result.
The Reviews tab opens on the timeline: every review, newest commit first, by month, with its summary and its notes' titles.
  • Reviews have a page each: the commit and author, the summary, then every note, marked with what it points at (PCB or schematic; red if it was removed) and coloured by its first tag. Newer and Older at the bottom step through the timeline.
  • Your own notes are any other Markdown files in reviews/ (design decisions, test results, ...), for example written in Obsidian. Frontmatter shows as properties, and tags: and #tags go to the Tags tab. [[links]] and [text](other-note.md) go to other notes, or to a review by its ID or its commit's message. Links to other files in reviews/ (a datasheet PDF, say) open them, and ![[picture.png]] embeds a picture.
  • It follows your system's light or dark theme, or the Theme button's choice.
A review's page: its notes, with On this page on the right. Search shows matches as you type.

docs.title: After a rebase, amend or squash
docs.text:
These replace commits with new ones (new hashes), so a review can be left pointing at a commit no branch has any more. Its file isn't touched, but the commit list no longer shows it as reviewed. A plain merge (or fast-forward) keeps the commits as they are, so nothing changes then.

When the GUI finds such reviews, it says so above the commit list:

  • Fix lists them. A rebase or amend keeps a commit's author and author date, so the commit it became is found by those and picked for you; press Move to point the review at it (notes pinned in that commit follow it too). If that commit has a review already, the two are merged.

  • A squash makes one new commit with a new date, so it can't be matched. Pick the squashed commit, press Review, then Bring in reviews: tick the reviews that went into it (those its message names, as git merge --squash and GitHub's "Squash and merge" do, are ticked already). Their summaries and notes are added to this review, and their files are removed when you press Write.

Git deletes replaced commits after a while (about a month), so a review you never move keeps its text but can no longer be matched automatically; Bring in still works.

docs.title: Schematic Viewer
docs.text:
The Schematic tab draws each sheet (wires, parts, labels, sheet boxes) with the same colours as the PCB: green added, red dashed removed, amber for parts whose value, footprint or connections changed, grey unchanged.

Action What it does Hover a wire, label or pin Highlight its net; the tooltip shows pins that joined or left, renames, or "wiring redrawn, connections unchanged" Hover a part Its changes: fields (value, footprint, MPN...), pins moved to other nets, moved Click Pin it; the card can jump to other sheets the net is on Double-click a sheet box Open that sheet (Backspace goes back up) Sidebar Sheet tree with change counts, and the changes on the current sheet

"Old positions" shows moved parts' previous place as a faint ghost (off by default).

docs.title: Nets
docs.text:
kigit works out the schematic's nets itself, across all sheets, buses (D[0..7], groups, aliases like USB_C{USB}) and KiCad 10's multiple top-level sheets. You can check them against KiCad's own netlist:

kicad-cli sch export netlist -o owl.net owl_v1.kicad_sch
kigit --check-netlist owl.net

docs.title: In the terminal
docs.text:
Every run also prints the schematic changes:

schematic: parts +1 -0, 8 changed electrically, 1 fields only, 0 only moved; 3 nets changed, 0 renamed, 1 only redrawn
  ~ J3     J3.1 (Pin_1): /owl_v1/CAN Transceiver/CAN_H -> GND, moved
  + R19    R          [IOs] on +3.3V, GND
  ~ C14    Footprint Capacitor_SMD:C_0402_1005Metric -> Capacitor_SMD:C_0603_1608Metric
  ~ net GND                      joined: J3.1 (Pin_1), R19.2  left: J3.3 (Pin_3)

Note

The drawing is kigit's own, not KiCad's export: close to KiCad but with a different font, and images and text boxes aren't drawn yet.

docs.title: Source Panel
docs.text:
The source panel shows the text of what changed in the .kicad_pcb / .kicad_sch files, old on the left and new on the right, like a side-by-side code diff. It sits under the drawing on both tabs.

It's off by default because it makes pages bigger:

kigit --source HEAD~1..HEAD

or tick Include source in the GUI.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
Removed lines are red, added lines green, and the changed part of a line is marked. Long unchanged stretches are folded (click to unfold).

Hover The panel shows A trace, via or pad Its own change first, then every other changed item on its net (and the net's pours) A pad of a moved or edited footprint The footprint's change first A footprint in the sidebar list That footprint A wire, label or pin (schematic) The net's changed wires and labels, on every sheet A part Its symbol's text A bus Its changed segments and bus labels

Each change says where it is (owl_v1.kicad_pcb:722 → :722), so you can find it in an editor.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
• Click pins the target, so you can move into the panel and scroll.
  • Drag its top edge to resize it.
  • The Source button collapses it.

Info

Only changed items' text goes into the page, not whole files. A pour's text stops before KiCad's computed fill polygons.
